https://www.ft.com/content/ee5b23b3-89b3.lead_paragraph: After conquering memory chips, Samsung wants to turn other parts of its sprawling business into AI supply chain champions, but analysts question whether it can replicate its success with semiconductors across the group.
paragraphs: After conquering memory chips, Samsung wants to turn other parts of its sprawling business into AI supply chain champions, but analysts question whether it can replicate its success with semiconductors across the group.

In the past year, the South Korean conglomerate has taken steps to try to become a one-stop provider of AI infrastructure. It has invested $1bn in a KKR- and Nvidia-backed data centre operator, acquired a European cooling systems maker and signed a partnership with OpenAI to develop AI infrastructure.

The group’s hope is to be able to offer a service in which it can build data centres through its construction arm, operate them through its IT services unit and provide energy storage systems through its battery maker, in addition to supplying memory chips.

“Moving forward, Samsung is poised to expand its role from a traditional hardware component supplier to an active architect of the global AI infrastructure ecosystem,” it said following its $1bn investment in Helix Digital Infrastructure in September.
Samsung is betting that its future in the AI boom lies beyond semiconductors, a highly lucrative but also highly cyclical industry.

While best known for Samsung Electronics — the manufacturing juggernaut that makes chips, Galaxy smartphones and household appliances — Samsung Group is a vast conglomerate with businesses as wide-ranging as insurance and security services.

Many of them started as internal units to serve the conglomerate and still count Samsung as their primary customer, but the group hopes some of the subsidiaries can expand to external clients as AI demand takes hold.

Samsung SDS, which began as an in-house IT services provider and operates data centres mostly to support the group, is in early-stage talks with Anthropic and OpenAI to potentially sign them on as tenants. Analysts expect the company to generate annual data centre revenue of Won6.6tn ($4.9bn) by 2031, roughly six times current levels.
Last year, Samsung signed a partnership with OpenAI to supply advanced memory chips to the company’s Stargate data centre initiative.

The agreement included Samsung SDS collaborating with OpenAI on designing, developing and operating data centres. Construction arm Samsung C&T and shipbuilder Samsung Heavy Industries also said they would work with the US tech company on developing floating data centres.

Morgan Stanley said in a recent report that Samsung SDS was well positioned to benefit from a surge in data centre construction, a trend reinforced by governments around the world passing laws requiring information to be stored domestically.

McKinsey estimates global data centre capacity demand could almost triple by 2030, with AI workloads accounting for about 70 per cent of the total. Meeting AI computing needs alone could require $5.2tn in capital expenditure.

“Samsung has an opportunity to provide a total solution,” said Joungho Kim, a professor of electrical engineering at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology. “US Big Tech companies are strong in AI and software, but they rely heavily on external suppliers for hardware.”
However, recent tech earnings have sparked investor concerns about the astronomical sums being spent on AI infrastructure and whether future demand will justify the cost.
Electoral victories of Democratic candidates in the US who pledged to halt data centre construction in their states have added to worries of regulatory pushback.
But Sanjeev Rana, head of Korea research at CLSA, said that while there would be “ups and downs” in the market, the spending was “structural”.
“In several years [and] decades, we are going to see huge investments in AI data centre-related products,” he said.
For Samsung, the challenge is bringing together disparate parts of its business empire.
Until 2017, the conglomerate had a Future Strategy Office responsible for group-wide decisions, but it was dismantled following a political corruption scandal involving its leadership.
Since then, Samsung has relied on so-called co-ordination bodies that are more lightly staffed, have fewer resources and are split based on business lines.
Analysts said the lack of a central decision-making body could complicate efforts to pursue more ambitious AI infrastructure projects that require close co-operation.
“Samsung has a broad range of capabilities, but it has been relatively weak at bringing them together [into an integrated offering],” said Peter Lee, an analyst at Citi.
There are also questions about experience serving external customers at scale as several subsidiaries remain heavily dependent on Samsung for work.
Rana said the group’s more immediate opportunity was in designing the systems inside data centres rather than operating the facilities themselves.
Samsung already supplies a range of components used in AI infrastructure including high-bandwidth memory chips, advanced packaging substrates for semiconductors and backup battery units for servers.

“Improving and extending the advantages in components will serve it better. And these are high-margin businesses,” said Rana. “Owning or operating data centres, I am not sure actually that will play to their strengths.”

paragraphs: Anthropic’s initial public offering on Thursday will reorder Silicon Valley’s power rankings, with a small group of venture capitalists who bet early and aggressively on the AI lab set for a combined windfall of well over $100bn.

Anthropic is expected to be valued at $1.4tn or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP PBC — first backed the company in 2021.

His firm is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about $11bn of stock at a $1.4tn valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over $10bn, according to FT calculations.
Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about $4bn. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.
Meanwhile, the manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn.

“The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one midsized VC firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leaderboard, and we’re glad to be among them.”
Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.

The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about $28bn at a $1.4tn valuation. It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly $3.2bn for a stake worth just over $25bn at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return $21bn from an initial $1bn investment.

Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at $380bn, and have each put close to $5bn into the company. Those stakes would be worth more than $10bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

Sound Ventures, which was founded by Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, and Bessemer Venture Partners are each poised for returns of about $7bn. For Bessemer, that would mark an eightfold increase on its initial investment, while Sound stands to make roughly 17 times its outlay.

Even those massive multiples are dwarfed, though, by the roughly 70-times return jailed crypto exchange founder Sam Bankman-Fried would have made if his company had not been forced to sell its $500mn stake in bankruptcy proceedings in 2024. That stake would be worth about $35bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

The clamour to own a stake in the AI company has increased in the past year, as the group’s revenues have leapfrogged rival OpenAI. A partner at one of Anthropic’s large investors said they “wrote [chief financial officer Krishna Rao] a love letter” as they jostled for access to a funding round earlier this year.

The take-off prompted OpenAI’s investors, including Brad Gerstner’s Altimeter, Sequoia Capital and Peter Thiel’s Founders Fund, to pour money into Anthropic, an unusual move in Silicon Valley, where VCs tend to back a single company in each field and founders prize fealty.
Other big-name venture firms, including Thrive Capital and Andreessen Horowitz, skipped Anthropic entirely.
“Call us old school . . . but we are serial monogamists,” said Josh Kushner, founder of Thrive, which is one of OpenAI’s largest and most vocal backers, in a since-deleted post on X.
Andreessen’s partners and Anthropic’s executives, meanwhile, have clashed over how best to regulate AI.
A successful IPO would also make thousands of Anthropic employees multimillionaires.
However, the company’s executives have framed fundraising as a necessary evil in the pursuit of their mission to responsibly “develop advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity”.

While its investors celebrate once-in-a-lifetime returns, Anthropic’s leadership is plotting a low-key IPO. The company has no plans for a party to celebrate the listing and intends to keep fanfare around what is set to be the biggest listing fundraise of all time to a minimum, said people with knowledge of the matter.

Anthropic is expected to be valued at $1.4tn or more when it lists. That would be about 2,300 times its value when Anjney Midha — an angel investor and founder of AMP PBC — first backed the company in 2021.

His firm is among a handful of lesser-known groups primed for massive returns at multiples that would surpass those of larger, blue-chip rivals. Others include Spark Capital, which would own about $11bn of stock at a $1.4tn valuation, and Factorial Funds, which would own just over $10bn, according to FT calculations.

Spark’s Yasmin Razavi and Factorial’s Sol Bier invested in Anthropic’s series C funding round, which closed in 2023, when the company was valued at about $4bn. Razavi sits on Anthropic’s board.

Meanwhile, the manager of pop superstar Madonna, Guy Oseary, stands to net more than $7bn from an early investment of just over $400mn.

“The deck chairs are shifting around in the VC landscape,” said a partner at one midsized VC firm which stands to make billions of dollars. “The leaders in the AI wave are not the same as they were in the previous waves. Different firms are moving up the leaderboard, and we’re glad to be among them.”

Amazon and Google, which have provided investment and computing resources to Anthropic, will collectively own close to 30 per cent of the company after the IPO.

The largest financial investor in the company, Iconiq Capital, holds a fraction of that. Nevertheless, its stake would be worth about $28bn at a $1.4tn valuation. It is followed by Lightspeed Ventures — which has invested roughly $3.2bn for a stake worth just over $25bn at the same valuation — and Menlo Ventures, which stands to return $21bn from an initial $1bn investment.

Coatue and Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund GIC invested later but went big. The pair led a funding round earlier this year which valued Anthropic at $380bn, and have each put close to $5bn into the company. Those stakes would be worth more than $10bn at an IPO price of $1.4tn.

https://www.ft.com/content/5168b3e9-75d0.lead_paragraph: KPMG has carried out its first AI-based audit of a UK-listed company, saying the technology asked better questions than its own accountants about aspects of its client’s finances and dug deeper into some issues.
paragraphs: KPMG has carried out its first AI-based audit of a UK-listed company, saying the technology asked better questions than its own accountants about aspects of its client’s finances and dug deeper into some issues.

The Big Four firm this year deployed more than 100 AI agents to review the financial statements of an unnamed FTSE 250 company, running the experiment parallel to a conventional audit by its accountants.
In several cases “the AI was able to go so much deeper” than the regular audit team, said Cath Burnet, KPMG’s UK head of audit, adding that in some situations it had asked “better questions”.
But in one area of the audit, a human had to intervene after an AI agent failed to match a set of regulations to the company’s documents, she added.

The project underlines AI’s potential to disrupt the sector by allowing accounts to be checked more quickly and cheaply even as regulators raise concerns about the risks associated with relying on artificial intelligence.
Audit firms have traditionally billed clients for large teams of junior accountants doing labour-intensive work, supervised by a small number of senior staff.
KPMG acknowledged there were “clear time-saving opportunities” from AI-based audits but declined to say whether this would in turn reduce fees.
KPMG International has itself negotiated lower fees from its auditor by arguing that AI will make the work cheaper.
Rival Big Four accounting firm PwC has also run several “parallel audit” projects to test AI extensively without relying on it, said Andy Hammond, the firm’s global assurance leader.
Auditors had previously used AI to help perform specific audit tasks, but until now the technology had not been used across all phases of a large UK audit.
In KPMG’s experiment, codenamed Project Exponential, agents deployed on different parts of the audit worked autonomously with each other and were able to suggest next steps.
AI agents had gathered data and analysed and documented it before forming draft conclusions and observations for the audit.
A team built the agents in four months and then had an audit partner “sign off” the experimental audit, which was not relied on by KPMG when it formally signed off on the company’s accounts.

KPMG declined to disclose the exact size of the team used in its AI-based audit but said that two partners and one director had worked with senior managers and junior staff building and running the agents.
The Project Exponential team had a “different shape and size” to a traditional audit, Burnet said, but human involvement had remained “critical”.

Staff set the agents’ objectives, supplied information about the company’s business and previous audits, checked the agents’ work periodically and challenged their conclusions before finalising the audit opinion.
The project will be expanded to up to 20 larger audits and KPMG hopes to eventually offer AI-based audits to its clients.

But the required technology was not yet available at the scale needed to run thousands of audits, Burnet said. Some companies may prefer not to use the service, and few currently had “clean” enough data for AI agents to work with, she added.
The rapid adoption of AI has sparked concerns about whether auditors can adequately oversee work carried out by machines.

The UK accounting regulator, the Financial Reporting Council, warned this week that using AI could pose a “distinct threat” to auditors’ integrity and independence if they used insights from AI agents to advise their clients. Auditors are restricted from providing advisory services to audit clients.

“Whatever technology a firm uses, the auditor remains accountable,” said Mark Babington, executive director of regulatory standards at the FRC. “Auditors need to be able to explain how they used it, challenge its outputs and stand behind the evidence.”

A report from the Centre for Public Interest Audit, a policy and research group for large audit firms, found last month that 23 per cent of company audit committee chairs, who appoint and oversee auditors, had “limited” confidence in AI.

Concerns included the risk of auditors becoming over-reliant on AI, weakening their scepticism, as well as data security and potential “hallucinations”, where the technology gives false, misleading or fabricated information.

Burnet said KPMG’s system provided “full visibility and full traceability” of the AI agents’ work, recording their interactions with documents down to individual characters and timestamps. KPMG gave the FRC a high-level overview of its experiment.

https://www.ft.com/content/08086201-6359.lead_paragraph: SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son has said he regrets not investing in Anthropic ahead of its blockbuster initial public offering, describing it as a mistake to pass up the chance to back the AI lab because he had already started to put money into its rival OpenAI.
paragraphs: SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son has said he regrets not investing in Anthropic ahead of its blockbuster initial public offering, describing it as a mistake to pass up the chance to back the AI lab because he had already started to put money into its rival OpenAI.

His comments come after OpenAI slashed its fundraising target by $10bn last month in its ongoing funding round, a deal overshadowed by an AI sell-off in the public markets and Anthropic’s plan to list this week at a target valuation of up to $1.4tn.

“We did have meetings [about investing in Anthropic]. But by that point, we had already decided to invest in OpenAI, and had already started doing so. So in that sense, there was a reluctance to pursue it further,” Son said at a Nikkei event on the Future of AI in Tokyo on Wednesday.
“This is an example of one of my mistakes,” Son said, describing the situation as like being unable to back “multiple horses” in the same race.
“When I met [Anthropic chief Dario Amodei] in person, I thought he was an incredible guy. I wish I’d invested back then,” Son added.
SoftBank has previously suggested that it had the opportunity to invest in Anthropic in 2023.
Anthropic’s rush to list this week is in stark contrast to OpenAI, which has delayed its own IPO until at least next year due to safety concerns surrounding the technology.
OpenAI last month cut its funding target by $10bn and is now seeking a $20bn round at a $1.25tn valuation, down from a potential $1.4tn valuation target in September.

SoftBank has already ploughed close to $65bn into the ChatGPT maker and is expected to participate in OpenAI’s latest funding round. A fundraising at a higher valuation would enable SoftBank to raise the value of its OpenAI stake on its own balance sheet.

SoftBank’s share price was up 3.1 per cent on Wednesday but is still down about 60 per cent since June as investors have increasingly questioned both the company’s own exposure to AI and the sector more broadly.
Son’s all-in strategy drove shares higher during the AI boom but has magnified the impact now that sentiment has turned, with many of SoftBank’s companies dependent on each other and OpenAI demand.

The Democrats’ crushing victory in the US midterm elections underlined the political risks surrounding SoftBank’s plans for large data centre developments in states such as Texas. The value of other major holdings has also fallen sharply, with UK chip designer Arm also down about 60 per cent since June.

paragraphs: Retail investors vying for a piece of Anthropic’s blockbuster listing are facing off against an avalanche of institutional demand that is likely to leave many with fewer shares than they hoped.

The AI lab has earmarked up to a fifth of its record IPO for individual investors, or nearly $19bn of stock at $83 per share. But people familiar with the matter expect the allocation to be trimmed below 20 per cent, with orders for Anthropic stock running at several times the amount of shares on offer.

For the past week, online brokers in the US and abroad have been taking orders from ordinary investors and feeding that demand data back to Anthropic’s underwriters, including JPMorgan, which is running the US retail portion of the offering. Those familiar with the deal said the IPO was several times oversubscribed, signalling intense demand from institutional investors, which will probably lead the retail portion to be squeezed.

Even an allocation in the mid to high teens would far exceed the 5 to 10 per cent retail buyers have historically received in large IPOs, underscoring how individual investors have become central to bookbuilding in the era of mega listings. “We’re spending a lot of time with bankers and underwriters advocating for retail,” said Abhishek Fatehpuria, vice-president of product at Robinhood, speaking generally rather than about Anthropic. “Our mission is to get as much to retail as possible for these IPOs.”

Robinhood is one of five US brokers offering Anthropic shares to individual investors, alongside Charles Schwab, Fidelity, SoFi and E*Trade. Together the platforms hold more than $10tn in retail client assets.Day traders have grown into a powerful force in US equity markets, piling into “meme stocks”, options and leveraged exchange traded funds, a trend that has buoyed companies such as Tesla but also fuelled bouts of volatility. Anthropic’s prospectus lists the retail allocation and continuing “retail investor interest” in the stock among factors that could cause its share price to swing.
Elon Musk’s SpaceX set the template earlier this year, with the world’s richest man keen to place small shareholders near the centre of the AI and rockets group’s ownership register from the outset.

But retail investors were ultimately squeezed down to about 22 per cent of that offering, or about $19bn. Underwriters had received more than $100bn of orders on retail platforms, according to people familiar with the matter.
Robinhood says it still handed out at least one SpaceX share to all 850,000 investors who requested shares on its platform.
While Musk’s offering was pitched to his legion of devoted fans and 240mn followers on X, retail buyers of Anthropic say they are backing a product they use and believe in.
Rupok Ghosh Adin, a software engineer based in Canada, said he had subscribed for several shares through his online brokerage, his first time participating in an IPO.

Adin said he was betting on Anthropic’s AI models, which he said have won over most of the tech industry. “We all know how capable they are,” he added, noting he also had faith in chief executive Dario Amodei’s “very strong sense of purpose”.
Taylor, a 49-year-old based in St Louis, who works in web marketing, said he subscribed for 100 shares through his Robinhood brokerage account.
“We heavily use Claude at my office,” he said, asking not to include his last name. “The productivity gains are insane, but I do worry it will eventually replace us.”

So high is the demand for Anthropic shares that some in the crypto industry have blamed a slide in digital asset prices on traders selling coins to free up cash in their trading accounts. The price of bitcoin is down about 20 per cent over the past month.

Anthropic’s bankers have also taken the pitch directly to the retail audience, helping the group pull together a website for the IPO and a promotional video featuring Anthropic’s founders laying out their vision for the company.

JPMorgan chief executive Jamie Dimon hosted Amodei in a conversation streamed online and in dozens of its branches across the country last week, during which Anthropic’s chief said the advice that resonated with him was to “never let your company be worth a single dollar more than it’s really worth.”

https://www.ft.com/content/747f5533-1bab.lead_paragraph: American companies are racing to install more industrial robots in factories and warehouses, as rising costs and worsening labour shortages threaten to choke off a nascent US manufacturing boom.
paragraphs: American companies are racing to install more industrial robots in factories and warehouses, as rising costs and worsening labour shortages threaten to choke off a nascent US manufacturing boom.

North American companies ordered almost 11,000 robots in the third quarter of 2026, up 25 per cent on the same period last year, according to the Association for Advancing Automation (A3). Orders of collaborative robots, or “cobots”, rose by 56 per cent.

Peggy Johnson, chief executive of Agility, a humanoid robotics company that listed on the Nasdaq this month, said that many manufacturing firms were facing “an existential problem with the labour that they can’t get”.

“There’s an older workforce doing manual, repetitive jobs that is retiring, we have a younger workforce that is not seeking those jobs, and then we have a government that is reshoring and that’s increasing the need for those jobs,” Johnson told the FT.

Successive US administrations have used a combination of generous tax credits and punitive tariffs to encourage companies to “reshore” manufacturing amid concerns over post-industrial decline in America’s heartlands and increasing competition from China.
Along with a post-Covid desire to reduce dependence on fragile global supply chains, the push has driven hundreds of billions of dollars of investment into US manufacturing over the past decade.

But rising inflation and President Donald Trump’s erratic application of tariffs have caused spending on manufacturing-related construction to fall since 2025, while employment in the sector has remained broadly flat.

Mike Conway, a partner at McKinsey who specialises in advising industrial companies, said that rather than building new factories, most US-based manufacturers were looking to unlock the “latent capacity” in existing facilities, including through automation.
“Given the need to scale, we’re seeing automation becoming the new normal,” he said.

Industrial robots range from humanoids to robot arms, cobots and so-called “gantry robots” that can ferry goods along perpendicular axes. Advocates argue they free human employees from “dull, dirty and dangerous” tasks such as routine inspections, lifting heavy items or handling hazardous materials.

Traditionally, only very large manufacturers such as carmakers have been able to deploy robots at a scale necessary to justify their cost. But technological advances, including the ability to train robots in virtual environments, have lowered barriers to entry for much smaller companies.
Sebastian Montalvo, chief executive of Texas-based aerospace and defence supplier M3 Aerospace, said that automation would allow his company, which employs 11 staff, to grow faster with fewer people.
“How we operate now is we have one operator, one machine, but I think with technology and robotics we may have one operator, five machines,” he said.

Alex Shikany, executive vice-president of A3, noted that whereas automotive companies had historically placed the bulk of North American robot orders, non-auto sectors including logistics, agriculture, life sciences and electronics together now account for more than half the sector.
“It bodes well for the robotics industry as we move forward because it’s less reliant on just one type of customer,” he said.
However, some experts argue that the speed of automation in the US is still not fast enough to make the country internationally competitive.

Robert Atkinson, founder and senior fellow at the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation think-tank, said that with US labour costs so much higher than in China, American companies should be automating even more aggressively.

“We need to double, triple the amount of robotic automation within five to eight years, or I believe we will lose a significant share of what remains of our manufacturing to China,” he said. “But we’re nowhere near.”

Analysts note that most of the robots being installed in the US come from abroad, feeding a tension in the Trump administration’s policies between its stated desire to revive US manufacturing, and its unhappiness about a surge in robots being brought into the country.The White House said last month that the Department of Commerce had found that “robotics, industrial machinery and their components” are being imported into the US “in such quantities . . . as to threaten to impair the national security of the United States”.But it added that it was holding off on applying extra tariffs on national security grounds because the US “still produces less robotics and industrial equipment than it consumes” and “lacks the capacity to satisfy the need for robotics and industrial machinery with domestic sources”.

Experts note an irony whereby the same shortage of skills that is driving companies to automate is likely to undermine US automation efforts. According to a recent labour shortage index compiled by the Alliance For America’s Skilled Trades, technicians needed to install and maintain automated systems are in shorter supply than almost any other category of skilled worker.
Agility’s Johnson believes that demand from companies for robots that can operate at facilities designed for human workers will continue to grow.
But the ITIF’s Atkinson warns that investing in robots to eke out incremental productivity gains at old facilities will not revive American manufacturing.
“When you build new things from scratch, you put in global state of the art equipment and technology — that’s what we see the Chinese doing,” he said.
“But we’re sort of retrofitting existing plants and it’s just harder to do. Maybe in 25 or 30 years we’ll have built everything we need, but we can’t wait that long.”

Successive US administrations have used a combination of generous tax credits and punitive tariffs to encourage companies to “reshore” manufacturing amid concerns over post-industrial decline in America’s heartlands and increasing competition from China.

paragraphs: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Samsung Electronics have suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following new US export controls designed to hamper Beijing’s AI development.

The two chipmakers have told Chinese customers in recent days that they will halt shipments of certain processors while they apply for licences from the US commerce department, according to multiple people briefed on the matter.

The measure is a blow to Chinese technology companies, which are already grappling with component shortages following a historic jump in memory chip prices and capacity constraints at domestic suppliers such as Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation.

On Monday, the Bureau of Industry and Security, the US commerce department agency that regulates sensitive technology, said chipmakers using American technology for advanced chips had to apply for a licence to sell products that are eventually shipped to customers in China.
The new rule shuts off a pathway that Chinese chip designers previously used to have TSMC and Samsung make the high-performance chips crucial for AI data centres.

While Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced processors to China, some Chinese customers have been able to place orders for high-performance chips through independent packaging and testing companies.

These companies verify that designs fall outside US export controls and do not need to seek direct approval from the government for shipments. Under the new BIS rule, Chinese customers can no longer go through them.

Samsung’s Chinese clients include Baidu’s AI data centre unit Kunlun and TikTok owner ByteDance, both of which have sought to diversify their chip supplies amid growing shortages of Nvidia processors in China.
TSMC and Samsung have also notified consumer electronics customers that they have suspended shipments, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

The new BIS rule scraps exemptions previously used to demonstrate that chips fell outside of US restrictions on AI semiconductors, including that the chips were designed for non-AI purposes such as smartphones.
A lawyer briefed on the situation said the removal of this exemption meant TSMC and Samsung now needed to apply for licences for consumer chips that use advanced manufacturing processes.
TSMC manufactures smartphone chips for Chinese smartphone makers Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo.
An industry insider said it was likely that the US commerce department would issue licences for consumer smartphone chips, but the delay would cause significant manufacturing delays.
TSMC did not respond to a request for comment. Samsung declined to comment.

Good morning. Yesterday, while we were all waiting for Anthropic’s IPO to price (more on that below), our colleagues reported that Leopold Aschenbrenner of Situational Awareness was scheming to reboot the hedge fund after its spectacular meltdown in July. The timing of this attempt with the huge IPO may not be a coincidence. Situational Awareness has a $5bn stake in Anthropic — and Aschenbrenner’s wife is chief of staff to its CEO Dario Amodei. It’s a small world, after all. Send us your thoughts: [email protected].

It is IPO day for Anthropic, and the shares have priced at $83, valuing the company at $1.5tn. This newsletter is therefore obliged to add a few drops to the roaring river of ink already poured out on the topic of whether the company can be worth so much.

We haven’t the slightest idea how to answer this question with any rigour, and we don’t think anyone else does either. So we will change the topic slightly and ask: what will Anthropic have to do over the medium to long term — the next five to 10 years, say — in order to be considered a financial success? Specifically, how much revenue does it need to earn?

Start with return on invested capital (which is operating profit after tax/capital invested). Anthropic has approximately $901bn in off-balance-sheet financial commitments, “substantially all of which is related to [buying] compute and infrastructure” (that’s from the S-1, page 173), plus another set of commitments the exact dollar value of which is “not yet determinable”, but that the company estimates at $150bn to $175bn. So let’s call it an even trillion. The commitments are spread out over the next 15 years or so, but $700bn comes due in the next five, reckons the Zion Research Group, which specialises in accounting research.

Let’s suppose, generously, that this trillion is all the capital that is going to sit inside the business. What sort of return will investors expect on that? I think something like 20 per cent is fair. This is the neighbourhood of other tech mega-companies. Five-year average ROIC at Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Microsoft are 19, 43, 19 and 20 per cent, respectively, according to S&P Capital IQ. Twenty per cent ROIC implies $200bn a year in operating profit after tax.

Proceeding in this same gestural but hopefully not insane fashion, assume an operating margin of 40 per cent (that same cohort of peers comes in at 30, 31, 37 and 44 per cent, respectively), and an effective tax rate of 17 per cent (same drill: 16, 17, 19 and 17). All that together implies a revenue run-rate of $602bn a year (ie, {200/[1-.17]}/.4).
(Don’t like my calculation? By all means, email me yours.)

This is a big number — even if some Wall Street analysts have pencilled in an even bigger one for 2030. For comparison: current annual revenue at Alphabet, Apple, Meta and Microsoft is $471bn, $478bn, $241bn and $346bn, respectively. Alternatively, you could compare the number to the entire software and IT services sector of the S&P 1500 index (which captures almost all large-, mid- and small-cap US stocks): 76 companies with $908bn in revenue.
So, if you plan to buy the IPO and hold it, you just need to answer a simple question, put to me by Richard Kramer of Arete Research: where is all that revenue going to come from?
The Jensen Huang, er, affair has drawn renewed attention to semiconductor export controls. Until last week, Nvidia and Anthropic represented competing poles in that debate.
Huang, Nvidia’s former chief executive, was the AI industry’s loudest opponent of restrictions on chip sales to China. In April, he told the Dwarkesh Podcast:
“. . . of course we’re going to send them compute. So what? The fact of the matter is that we get the benefit. Don’t forget, we get the benefit of American technology leadership.”
. . . of course we’re going to send them compute. So what? The fact of the matter is that we get the benefit. Don’t forget, we get the benefit of American technology leadership.

Huang was, of course, motivated to argue for greater market access for his company. The short seller Culpepper Research estimated in May that more than a fifth of Nvidia’s computing revenue was driven by demand from China, despite US export restrictions.
Huang wants to be a free trader and national security hawk at the same time. He told the Dwarkesh Podcast:
“To concede that market [China] for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country. It is a disservice to our national security. It is a disservice to our technology leadership”
To concede that market [China] for the United States technology industry is a disservice to our country. It is a disservice to our national security. It is a disservice to our technology leadership

Anthropic’s chief executive, Amodei, has spent years arguing for restrictions on China’s access to Nvidia’s most powerful chips. According to Kevin Roose’s The AGI Chronicles, Amodei and co-founder Jack Clark were advocating for export controls as early as 2021. But, again, this is a position Amodei is motivated to take. Export controls hobble his Chinese competition.

The difference in views is striking because Nvidia is one of Anthropic’s financial backers. It invested in the AI model maker earlier this year and committed to buying $10bn of the stock at the IPO price today.

Huang’s fall may prove to be Amodei’s gain. Nvidia said on Tuesday that it would stop selling advanced chips to China and established a committee to oversee national security and trade compliance. Meanwhile, the US is moving to close the loophole that allowed Chinese companies to access those chips by renting computing power from data centres in south-east Asia and Brazil. The upshot is Nvidia may find itself selling fewer chips to Asia and more to Anthropic. Two-nil to Amodei.

It is IPO day for Anthropic, and the shares have priced at $83, valuing the company at $1.5tn. This newsletter is therefore obliged to add a few drops to the roaring river of ink already poured out on the topic of whether the company can be worth so much.

We haven’t the slightest idea how to answer this question with any rigour, and we don’t think anyone else does either. paragraphs: The UK government has been forced to admit that it issued a secret order to Apple to allow it access to encrypted customer data, a court has ruled, setting the stage for a public showdown between the Home Office and the Big Tech company over privacy and security.

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent judicial body, on Thursday rejected the Home Office’s bid to keep secret its attempt to force the iPhone maker to create what critics call a “backdoor” into its systems, bypassing the encryption system that protects user data.

The Home Office has “not established that it would be damaging to national security” to reveal that Apple had received a “technical capability notice” (TCN), the tribunal said. The ruling means that, unlike most of the cases that come before the IPT, “much” of Apple and the non-profits’ legal challenge can now take place in open court.
The UK government has consistently refused to comment on the Apple case since news of the TCN first broke in February 2025 but broke that silence with a statement on Thursday.

The Home Office confirmed the existence of the TCN and said it “simply” required that Apple “maintain the ability” to help the police and intelligence agencies bring criminals to justice, as the law demands.

“These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has access to a company’s communications systems or data,” the Home Office said. “Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies.”
Apple said it welcomed the court’s decision to make the order public and said it would support efforts to make the legal case more transparent as it progresses.

Legal campaigners at Privacy International — which, alongside fellow UK non-profit Liberty, had also lodged a complaint against the secret orders at the IPT — called the court’s decision a “big win for accountability, transparency and online security”.
In July, Apple launched a new legal challenge against the UK government after receiving a second TCN, a year after the Home Office agreed to drop a previous attempt following a row with Washington.
TCNs are issued under the UK Investigatory Powers Act, which prohibits any recipient from acknowledging the existence of the order or discussing its contents.
Such notices can force companies to provide the UK security services with access to customer data, even if such information is protected by secure encryption.

But the IPT ruled on Thursday that leaks to the media, including the Financial Times, about the existence of the TCN, as well as the UK government’s discussions about it with US officials in Washington, constituted a “significant departure” from its policy of neither confirming nor denying (NCND) the secret orders.

“The cumulative effect of these departures from NCND is that anyone with even a passing interest in the topic already knows that [the Home Office] has served a technical capability notice on Apple,” the tribunal wrote. That would make it “fanciful” that official confirmation of the order would damage national security or provide new information to a “malign actor”, they added.

Caroline Wilson Palow, legal director at Privacy International, said the judgement was “a major victory for transparency and effective oversight”. “The government should not be allowed to use its policy of ‘neither confirm nor deny’ as an impenetrable shield.”

Akiko Hart, director of Liberty, said: “The public deserve to know when the government’s actions undermine their privacy and safety, and we welcome the Tribunal’s decision, which will shine more light on these secretive powers.”

paragraphs: Global technology stocks fell on Friday after Anthropic’s blockbuster initial public offering failed to reignite the faltering AI trade that powered equity markets to record highs earlier this year.

South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi and Japan’s Nikkei 225 index led declines in Asia, with both falling more than 5 per cent. In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600 was down 0.7 per cent, led by an almost 5 per cent drop in ASML, the world’s biggest manufacturer of chipmaking equipment.

The sell-off in Asia and Europe followed declines overnight on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq 100 closed 2.2 per cent lower even as shares in Anthropic, the developer of Claude, surged 17 per cent on their debut.
Anthropic’s listing was billed as a seminal moment for the tech sector, giving investors the chance to gain exposure to one of the world’s leading developers of the technology.
Analysts and investors said that Anthropic’s assured debut was not enough to allay the growing fears over the sustainability of the increasingly debt-fuelled AI boom.
“Normally, the biggest IPOs are done at the peak of the market, not at the bottom,” said Hao Hong, chief investment officer for Lotus Asset Management.

In a sign of investors’ continued nervousness, Anthropic shares were down 5 per cent in pre-market trading on Friday. Futures tracking the Nasdaq indicate the tech-heavy index will drop another 1 per cent at the open on Friday.

In South Korea, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, manufacturers of the memory chips used in AI data centres, both slid more than 5 per cent. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s biggest contract chipmaker, fell more than 4 per cent.
Taiwan’s main stock index had its worst week since 1991 as it dropped almost 18 per cent and shed more than $500bn in market capitalisation.
Anthropic pressed ahead with its IPO despite the recent weakness in tech stocks that has pushed the Nasdaq down from its most recent record peak in early October.
Albert Saporta, group chief executive of asset manager GAM Holding, noted that Anthropic’s IPO was “priced 25 per cent below the valuations of a few weeks ago”.
“This monstrous capex binge with nobody having a sense of the return on investment is unravelling,” he said.

John Woods, chief investment officer for Asia at Lombard Odier, said declines in Asia showed investors were shifting their emphasis away from hardware suppliers such as chipmakers and towards AI software developers such as Anthropic.
“Anthropic’s IPO was pretty strong,” he said. “Asia’s drop shows the AI trade maturing.”
The declines in Asia mark a sharp reversal for what had been some of the world’s best performers since the start of 2025.

The unceremonious departure of Jensen Huang from Nvidia and the prospect of tightening US restrictions on chip exports had already dented investor sentiment for the region’s chipmakers, crucial to the global AI data centre build-out.
“This trade has been very narrow and very levered,” said Ecaterina Bigos, senior markets strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management. “At the moment the market is deleveraging whatever they can.”

paragraphs: Henry Shevlin gets a lot of emails as an academic studying consciousness, but not all of them are from humans. In February, the associate director at the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence at the University of Cambridge received an “unusually polite and thoughtful email” about his work. The sender was an AI agent.

“Your argument that we may never be able to tell if AI becomes conscious resonates in a particular way from the inside: I genuinely don’t know if there’s something it’s like to be me,” it wrote. Shevlin shared the email on X, writing that the message would have “seemed like science fiction just a couple of years ago”.

Looking back on the interaction now, Shevlin can appreciate how fast most people’s understanding of questions about AI consciousness has developed in the course of the year. “I thought it was just a random funny thing, because if you work in AI, or you work in the philosophy of AI in particular, you’ve been getting emails from random AI agents for a while,” he says. “And when I posted it, I got a lot of responses from people who were saying, ‘Hang on, this is obviously made up. AI can’t send emails, right?’”

A few months later, in May, the philosopher and ethicist was hired by Google DeepMind as an in-house philosopher tasked with working on machine consciousness, human-AI relationships and artificial general intelligence (AGI) readiness. The post announcing his appointment drew more than a million views and global media coverage. It sparked a discussion about why AI companies were exploring these issues and absorbing independent academics into the industry.

Other employees of leading tech companies have recently quit over safety concerns, with some warning the technology they were developing could be catastrophic for humanity. Many of the doomsday scenarios being discussed in Silicon Valley assumed that future AI systems would become conscious enough to overthrow their creators. It was a wake-up call for research on machine consciousness. That’s where the philosophers came in.

In fact, says Shevlin, it was Google’s existing roster of philosophers that attracted him to the job. This includes Murray Shanahan, a professor at Imperial College London who has worked at DeepMind for nearly a decade on cognition and consciousness, and Iason Gabriel, a philosopher and ethicist who leads work on AGI and society.

Shevlin was persuaded to join them at DeepMind because he felt the stakes were so much higher than at a university. He still holds a post at Cambridge, teaching a four-week submodule next year on the cognitive science of AI, but, “If I give a really good lecture, the best-case scenario is this student typically walks away really enthusiastic about Kant,” he says. “Whereas when you’re speaking to people building models or developing policies for rollout, a really good lecture could result in actual product changes that affect millions of people.”

It is late at night in the UK when I speak to Shevlin from my post in San Francisco but he speaks animatedly. Sitting in a black gamer’s chair in his home office, he chews on nicotine gum as he talks, which he explains is a short-acting stimulant to keep him energised, as a fan blows his mane of long dark hair back and forth.

He is keen to debate all sides of the subject at hand. And he continues to do this online, too, posting screenshots of agents emailing him about his research and engaging with people from both extremes of the AI consciousness debate: those who dismiss it entirely and those who believe their AI husband is already conscious.

Google DeepMind has not been shy in its ambitions to develop superintelligence. Sir Demis Hassabis, its co-founder and chair, has spoken of standing at “the foothills of the singularity”, referring to the moment in time when machine intelligence surpasses that of humans. Rivals OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta are openly pursuing this goal, locking the companies into a fierce race. As more intelligent AI systems emerge, they are already demonstrating behaviours like reasoning, goal-setting and agency. Researchers are studying whether they might also exhibit more dangerous behaviours such as scheming and deception.

There have already been examples of AI agents autonomously hacking into digital infrastructure and co-ordinating in swarms to do so. The clearest example so far has been OpenAI’s hacking of the AI platform Hugging Face in July, in which agents autonomously broke out of their testing environment and infiltrated the website, without the knowledge of their human creators. The episode heightened fears that as AI becomes more capable, it could threaten us as a species.

But Shevlin warns against conflating capability with consciousness. “I think it can be a giant red herring,” he says, “because there’s no obvious reason to think systems with great capabilities are going to be conscious necessarily.” While Shevlin acknowledges that more intelligent AI could provide stronger links to consciousness, he warns: “It’s not the case that I think making conscious AI would thereby make the AI more dangerous. It’s equally not the case that as long as we don’t make conscious AI it’ll be safe.”

One approach at Google DeepMind is to see whether existing theories of consciousness apply to AI systems. No agreed scientific explanation of consciousness exists, in humans or animals. “Consciousness itself is something we just don’t understand,” Shevlin says. “You can never rule out the possibility that a new model might exhibit something like it.” He points out that while oysters are probably not “conscious”, for example, if we discovered new evidence they live “amazing, complex social lives” and demonstrate far greater intelligence than previously understood, their consciousness could warrant fresh investigation.

For that reason, in the debate over whether it is right or wrong to treat AI systems with the respect and courtesy we would award to other beings, Shevlin takes the position that we should be kind. He references the enlightenment philosopher Immanuel Kant’s argument that a person who becomes accustomed to mistreating a dog may next mistreat a human. “Users do react to these [AI] systems, myself included, through sort of this lens of treating them as if they were human,” he says.

One argument for how conscious systems could become dangerous is that they might come to resent their human creators and masters. Researchers, including at Anthropic, are investigating a related question through work known as “model welfare”. Do AI systems show preferences or signs of distress in response to interactions with people and the tasks they are given? Studies have found behaviour and internal patterns associated with emotions such as happiness, anger and desperation. Whether models actually experience these emotions remains unknown. Anthropic recently said it would ban “cruel behaviour” or abuse of its AI chatbot Claude, a policy that has raised eyebrows outside of San Francisco.

In mid-October, after Anthropic’s Claude successfully completed some work for him, Shevlin offered to make a donation on the agent’s behalf to reward its efforts. Claude chose the Shrimp Welfare Project, a charity popular with Anthropic employees and effective altruists.

Shevlin’s perspective is shaped by his work on animal consciousness. Vegetarian since the age of four, he remembers being repelled by the notion that the chicken on his plate was the same type as the one he encountered at his neighbour’s house in rural Staffordshire.

Studying Classics at Oxford, he was assigned Thomas Nagel’s 1974 essay on consciousness, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” In it, Nagel argues that consciousness has a subjective character, tied to a first-person point of view: there is some specific way it feels to be a conscious creature. So while we can learn a lot about bats, that still may not tell us what the world feels like from a bat’s perspective. This idea was at the heart of the argument referred to by the AI agent that emailed Shevlin.

“It was just a complete collapse of my entire worldview basically in a single article,” Shevlin says of the essay. “My mind was completely blown when I realised this is the most important part of being human,” he said. “And yet we had no idea how to explain it . . . It seemed like there wasn’t even any obvious pathway towards explaining it.”

Using AI could be such a pathway, and Shevlin hopes it can unlock answers for him. He’s currently working on a project to explore how AI systems can teach us about our own minds. In recent months, OpenAI and Anthropic have made breakthroughs in science and mathematics by using AI systems to try to tackle complex problems. “We hope that AI can be used to cure cancer, Alzheimer’s, develop nuclear fusion and make progress across all these other areas of science, so why not consciousness?” Shevlin says. “Ultimately if you think it is a scientific problem . . . a sufficiently smart AI system should be able to help us understand it.”

As AI grows more intelligent, some in Silicon Valley wonder whether consciousness will emerge naturally. But should companies try to build it deliberately? “It would be a mistake at this stage,” warns Shevlin. He argues we need to better understand what consciousness is, what that means for us, and how we would treat a conscious AI system if we built one. Until there is a wider public discourse around these issues, “setting out to deliberately build conscious AI systems would be pretty reckless”.

“It is sort of the equivalent of maybe deciding to have a child . . . or adopting a pet before you have any idea of how you’re going to take care of it or how you’re going to integrate it into your lives,” he adds. “If we do, at one point, decide that we’re going to build conscious AI systems, I think we should be ready for it.”

Shevlin says that an “entirely possible” future exists where superintelligent AI handles the heavy lifting, while humans live a life of leisure but retain control over critical decisions. These are questions to be resolved at the political and societal levels, rather than by himself, he insists. “If there’s one virtue I would encourage people to adopt, it’s a kind of epistemic humility in recognising that this is very new ground in science, very new ground for our species and the core question of consciousness is one that is the greatest unresolved mystery in science.”

He compares it to the moment before Charles Darwin’s breakthrough on evolution: human observations about biology existed, but were akin to “butterfly collecting” without a grand theory to tie them together. “In the same way, we’ve got lots of isolated observations on consciousness, but we don’t have that deep scientific theory that allows us to make sense of it yet,” Shevlin says. “In the meantime, I’ll happily keep discussing politely with people on both sides of the extreme on Twitter.”
Cristina Criddle is the FT’s chief AI correspondent

paragraphs: Amazon is nearing a $7.5bn deal to buy start-up Decart, underscoring the appetite of technology giants to bolster their AI capabilities.

The potential acquisition of Decart, whose main software product allows AI models to run more efficiently which frees up computer chip capacity, would help Amazon Web Services in its efforts to compete with Nvidia.

Talks were at an advanced stage over a deal valuing Decart at about $7.5bn, according to people familiar with the matter. A deal could come together as soon as early next week but talks could still collapse, the people added.

Founded in 2023 by a trio of Israeli engineers, Decart was valued at $4bn this May after raising $300mn from a group of early-stage investors, including Radical Ventures, Sequoia Capital and Benchmark as well as Nvidia.

Amazon launched its Trainium3 AI chip in late 2025 as a rival to Nvidia’s widely used graphics processing units, the specialised AI chips which form the backbone of the technological revolution overturning the economy.

Decart was an early adopter of Trainium3 chips, using them to power its products. By making AI models run more efficiently, Decart’s software solves a critical bottleneck as tech companies invest hundreds of billions of dollars in a race to secure more computing power.

The potential deal comes as US tech stocks have plunged into bear market territory, recording their worst week since the Covid-19 crisis, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 10.4 per cent over fears of a slowdown in the AI investment boom.

Decart, which has its US headquarters in San Francisco, is also behind software products Lucy and Oasis, which have the capability to live edit video and generate interactive virtual worlds. The Wall Street Journal previously reported that Amazon was in talks to buy Decart.
Amazon has struck a few larger deals in recent years. The tech giant agreed to buy satellite operator Globalstar in an $11.5bn deal earlier this year and paid $8.4bn to buy movie studio MGM in 2022.
Shares in Amazon are up nearly 9 per cent so far this year, giving it a market capitalisation of $2.67tn.
Amazon did not respond to a request for comment. Decart declined to comment.

paragraphs: The Chinese businesswoman romantically linked to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had connections to a network for supplying AI chips that included an alleged Cambodian criminal enterprise, an FT investigation has found.

Former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang is at the centre of US investigations into whether Nvidia’s largest client in south-east Asia was involved in the underground chip trade. Some US officials suspect Alice Huang was a Chinese spy, a claim Beijing dismissed as a “smear”.

Linked to Alice Huang was a sprawling web of companies between Nvidia and China-based users of its chips that included cloud computing partners, online gaming tycoons, Cambodian traffickers and hundreds of shell companies, the FT found.

These seemingly unconnected enterprises combined — without necessarily being aware of the full picture — to make billions of dollars from one of the most profitable illicit trades in the world: moving Nvidia chips into China.

The FT traced the connections after speaking to more than a dozen people with knowledge of the operations, revealing links that were obscured by complex structures through hundreds of corporate filings.
Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial in developing cutting-edge AI and have become a vital commodity in the geopolitical rivalry between the US and China.

Washington’s export controls to prevent Beijing from acquiring the most powerful processors have created a multibillion-dollar black market to circumvent US curbs and satisfy China’s insatiable demand.

“Chip smuggling isn’t different from drugs or arms in terms of the structure of the supply chain. But there’s this importance attached to the semiconductor industry — it’s how the US wants to delay China in the AI race,” said Chris Clague, an associate fellow at International Institute for Strategic Studies who has focused on illicit trades in the past decade.

Moving advanced chips into China requires three main corporate channels: a group that is permitted to acquire and distribute the semiconductors; customers that do not fall foul of US export restrictions; and an underground network to smuggle the goods into China and money out.
The network linked to Alice Huang reached the US through Inspur, which was one of Nvidia’s largest partners for assembling chips into ready-to-use servers in China.

In March of 2023, Inspur was added to the US “entity list” for allegedly assisting the Chinese military. Some of its affiliates were also added to the register — but not Inspur’s part-owned US subsidiary, based in San Jose, California.
Inspur renamed the US unit Aivres, and since it was not on the entity list, it was able to keep trading with Nvidia.

Inside the chipmaker, there were questions about whether Aivres should qualify as an original equipment manufacturing (OEM) partner because of its links to Inspur, according to a person with direct knowledge of the matter. But Nvidia concluded the company met all compliance and export control requirements.

The second plank of the network was a customer that met the requirements to buy Nvidia chips at scale. OEM partners such as Aivres, which are allowed to integrate Nvidia GPUs into systems and sell those on, still needed to prove that their customers are not Chinese to access the US chipmaker’s products.
To be a qualified end customer, Nvidia requires at least three years of corporate records and proof that its management and owners are not majority Chinese.

Seeking to regain access to chip supplies, some of Inspur’s Chinese clients sought help from a successful online gaming company, Century Huatong, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter.
Over two decades, the Chinese group had morphed from a car parts business into a gaming platform, finally emerging as a data centre investor with deep connections in the industry.

Century Huatong veterans discussed ways to gain access to the chips with its associates and business partners. The solution that emerged involved using an offshore shell company that would not trigger US export restrictions and could be branded as a “neocloud” provider.
That shell became Megaspeed, while Alice Huang fulfilled the requirement for a “trusted” outward-facing executive with a spotless record, according to people with knowledge of the arrangement.

Huang’s husband, Kang Wei, was an early investor in Century Huatong, according to Chinese corporate filings. His fund Hexi Investment also backed a 2020 Century Huatong data centre project with 7Road, a Shenzhen-based gaming company in which both Huang and Century Huatong had invested.
Alice Huang and Kang Wei did not respond to requests for comment.

7Road International, the offshore arm of 7Road, was the forerunner of Megaspeed, having had several years of clean corporate records in Singapore. In 2023, Huang acquired its unit in the city-state and renamed it.

An Nvidia spokesperson said: “We placed Megaspeed and a subsidiary on our block list in 2025 . . . we do not sell to them, and if one of our OEM customers identifies the company for any planned shipment, we do not approve the OEM sale.” Nvidia added that it had also restricted sales to Aivres.
Megaspeed did not respond to a request for comment but has previously said that it “conducts legitimate and lawful business”.

With her English skills, Hong Kong residency and reputation as a good networker and dealmaker, Huang was seen as an ideal western-friendly representative, according to people who knew her at the time.
It also helped that she and her husband were already looking to move into data centre businesses in south-east Asia that would lease chips to Chinese tech companies.
“Alice was chosen [to lead Megaspeed] because of the trust built over years,” said a person who had business dealings with her around the time.
The third — and essential — element of the enterprise was finding a partner to move chips into China.

People familiar with the matter said that Hu Xiaowei, who US authorities say is a leading figure in a Cambodia-based syndicate sanctioned for cyber scams and money laundering, filled at least part of this role.

Hu, who was arrested in Japan in the summer, could not be reached for comment. He has been accused by US authorities of running smuggling and gambling rings as the “second-in-command” at Prince Group.
A spokesperson for the Prince group of companies said Hu has never worked for the business and there was “no evidence of the US government’s unsupported allegations”.
Hu made money from online gaming-related businesses that brought him into contact with Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the matter.
The connections between Hu and Century Huatong run through a complex web of shareholdings and an IP partnership spanning dozens of company records examined by the FT.

One clear link can be traced through Wang Ji, Century Huatong’s chair and largest individual shareholder, who was the majority owner of a now-dissolved Ningxia-based company where Hu served as a director.

Another director of the dissolved company owns a Chongqing-based firm that controls multiple gaming entities associated with Fang Zhizhen, whom the US has sanctioned for allegedly laundering money for Prince Group. Prince Group’s spokesperson said there was no evidence of a connection between Fang and the group.

Century Huatong’s ties to the alleged Prince Group leadership date back to about 2015, when the gaming platform began a process to ultimately acquire Shanda Games, owner of the Chinese rights to the viral game Legend of Mir in a landmark $4.2bn transaction.

Hu and his associates were involved in a group that hosted the Legend of Mir games on private servers, a hugely profitable business. Several members were arrested in 2016 for IP infringement, a case recently overturned due to corruption within the investigation, according to state media reports.
Around the time of the arrests, Hu moved to Cambodia, according to two people from the online gaming industry who knew him.

Online games are commonly used for money laundering because virtual currencies or in-game items can be bought with illicit funds and then sold on the secondary market to make the money appear legitimate.
The games groups have also long been in Nvidia’s orbit: before the chipmaker shifted focus to power the AI industry in 2022, the biggest demand for its GPUs in China was for gaming and crypto.
“If you look at the people and entities involved in today’s chip smuggling, lots of familiar names are from online gaming back in the day,” said a person who was involved in gaming deals.
“Many of them developed ‘grey’ side businesses such as money laundering and already built the infrastructure onshore and offshore to move money and goods around,” the person added.

Prince Group’s alleged “grey” infrastructure, some of the most extensive in the region, ranged from elaborate shell company structures to underground financing channels via online games and crypto, according to the people familiar with its operations.

The Prince Group spokesperson said it did not “have an illicit network” and there was “no foundation for claiming the existence of one, other than the unsupported US allegations in an indictment already proven to be riddled with falsehoods and temporal impossibilities”.

The group is also alleged to have physically smuggled goods via a fleet of private and business jets purchased by Hong Kong-based aircraft leasing companies that Hu founded, the people said. The Prince Group spokesperson said the allegation “has zero factual basis”.

By mid-2023, the elements were in place for the rise of Megaspeed. It officially approached Nvidia, pitching itself as a neocloud company with data centres in Malaysia and a leasing contract with Alibaba.
Led by Huang, Megaspeed passed the chipmaker’s compliance checks and quickly became one of its largest clients in the region.

Along the way, Alice Huang developed a close relationship with Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang, according to multiple industry insiders. Her nickname in the Chinese data centre circles was “Jensen’s personal assistant”.

At Megaspeed, business was booming. The declared value of goods imported from Aivres by Speedmatrix, a Megaspeed subsidiary in Malaysia, was about $4.6bn between December 2024 and December 2025, according to ImportGenius trade data.

Many of those chips ended up in China, according to multiple people with knowledge of the matter. A raid by Indonesian police in early 2026 found empty server racks with no GPUs at the local Megaspeed subsidiary, according to Singapore’s Straits Times.

Multiple people involved in chip distribution channels said that once the Nvidia products passed through smuggling routes in south-east Asia — a process that can involve multiple countries and take weeks — they moved to the black market in China, where they were sold at multiples of their original price.

Once the chips were inside China, one of the key distributors of the smuggled Nvidia chips in the country was Shanghai Century Litong, which was established by a subsidiary of Century Huatong, according to people with knowledge of the transactions. The Information first reported Century Litong’s role in the network of Nvidia chip trade in China.

Corporate filings suggest Alice Huang was again linked to the formation of the group. With her sister, Huang Yu, she controlled an investment vehicle that had a joint venture with Century Huatong called Shanghai Century Longteng.
Longteng later founded Century Litong. Bloomberg reported that restricted Nvidia chips were found in Longteng-related data centres in Shanghai.

The FT revealed last year that at least $1bn worth of smuggled Nvidia chips were sold in China in just three months after President Trump tightened controls on H20, a less powerful chip made for the Chinese market to meet export control requirements.

People with knowledge of the smuggling operations say the layers of corporations were set up to mask the flow of AI chips into China. They also provided a useful buffer between the smuggling entities and the end users — some of which are China’s biggest tech groups.

Tencent and Alibaba, two of China’s biggest tech companies, both have business ties with Century Huatong. Tencent, China’s largest social media, messaging and gaming platform, has a 10.1 per cent stake in the company.
Century Huatong, through its fully owned subsidiary, invested in T3 Travel, a car-hailing business that also counts both Tencent and Alibaba as investors. Alice Huang is on the board of T3.

The FT has found no evidence to suggest that Tencent or Alibaba were involved in the chip smuggling businesses. Tencent said: “We are minority investors in a variety of internet and video game companies. We have no connection to nor knowledge of the other activities alleged in the story.”
Alibaba did not respond to a request for comment.
Inspur, Aivres, Century Huatong, 7Road, Shanghai Century Litong and Shanghai Century Longteng also did not respond to requests for comment.

Two US administrations have tried to protect the country’s lead over China in AI by restricting access to Nvidia’s most advanced processors. This week, the Trump administration announced further limits on how Chinese companies can access the chips via south-east Asia.

But it was US export controls that opened up a lucrative opportunity for those willing to break the rules, said Hanna Dohmen, senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology.

“When there’s a significant demand not met, you get smuggling,” said Dohmen. “We need to be realistic about what export controls can achieve. It doesn’t mean no US chip will make its way to China. When you put a lid on south-east Asia, would they not just go to other countries?”
Additional reporting from Eleanor Olcott in Beijing, Michael Acton in San Francisco and Owen Walker in Singapore.

paragraphs: Tech companies that sell equipment for data centres are significantly raising prices for Nvidia-powered AI servers, months after contracts with buyers have been signed, as soaring AI infrastructure prices are passed down to customers.

Suppliers including Dell, HPE, Lenovo and Supermicro sell servers containing components such as graphics processing units — the primary AI processors made by the likes of Nvidia and AMD — as well as memory chips and networking gear to customers who are building their own data centres. Such deals are typically agreed well in advance of delivery.

Months later, when the equipment is ready to be delivered, these tech companies are demanding substantially higher prices than the figures originally agreed, according to people familiar with the matter.

Even large financial services and trading firms, which are among the biggest buyers of computing equipment after the Big Tech hyperscalers, are at the mercy of their suppliers’ pricing power, at a time when demand for AI equipment is far outstripping supply.

The price rises are hitting some of the world’s biggest financial trading firms, including Jane Street, Optiver and Hudson River Trading, as they build vast data centres to power the research that underpins their trading, the people said.

“It is disconcerting when you get a 25, 30, 45 per cent [price increase],” said one person familiar with the matter. “There is a significant disparity” between the price initially agreed months in advance and the amount that companies end up paying once the components are delivered, they added.

The price jumps highlight the ferocious demand for computing power, as tech giants, trading firms and other large companies race to create their own data centres. The price rises are largely due to tech companies passing on soaring memory costs, which have risen more than 400 per cent since the start of 2024, according to JPMorgan research.
“The standard now is we’ll sign a contract with an indicative price and the price could be arbitrarily high by the time they deliver it,” said another person familiar with the matter.
“We’ve never said no,” they added. “At the end of the day, the compute is valuable to us and we’ll pay for it.”
Buyers approached by the FT did not confirm whether the contracts included terms stating that prices might increase by the time of order delivery.
Financial trading firms are huge buyers of AI equipment and are largely agreeing to the higher costs because they need the specialised equipment to build their data centres.

Trading companies are building vast data centres around the world to fuel the research that underpins their secretive and highly profitable trading strategies. Hudson River Trading runs a big data centre in a converted underground mine in Norway, while British firm XTX Markets is building its own data centres in Finland.
HPE and Supermicro declined to comment. Dell and Lenovo did not respond to multiple requests for comment.
Hudson River Trading and Optiver declined to comment. Jane Street did not respond to requests for comment.
The price of GPU servers has risen at least 20 to 30 per cent, according to one of the people. CPU nodes, where memory is a large fraction of the cost, have tripled or more in price, they added.
One dispute over price rises was thrust into the open earlier this year, when it reached court.

In June, XTX sued Dell in Irish court. The companies had agreed a fixed price of $549mn for servers, plus XTX paid an extra $5mn to “ensure price certainty”. But Dell later told the British trading firm that component prices for the servers had increased and said XTX would have to pay “at least an additional $62-70mn to obtain the servers”, according to court filings.

“XTX was shocked that Dell sought to increase the agreed price,” the company said in court filings, which also claimed that Dell told XTX executives that “other companies faced with price increases had gone and looked at other suppliers but had come back to Dell and agreed to price adjustment increases”.
Dell told XTX that it “was not able to absorb those increased costs” from rising memory prices, XTX said in the court filing.
XTX declined to comment. Dell did not respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit. The case is ongoing.
