The attacks have escalated sharply in recent months, with a wave of breaches targeting ports, oil tankers and shipping giants. The increasingly sophisticated threats are being carried out by cybercriminals and groups linked to hostile states, exposing vulnerabilities in the ageing networks that enable international commerce. At the Port of Corpus Christi in Texas, the largest US gateway for crude oil exports totalling around 2.3mn barrels per day, executives say hackers are probing their systems hundreds or even thousands of times a day, attempting to penetrate networks and trick employees into handing over access.The attacks can vary from automated attempts to guess passwords and overwhelm computer networks to more sophisticated intrusions meant to steal or erase data.

Experts link countries like Iran, North Korea and China to hacking operations targeting shipping infrastructure. Cybersecurity company Shieldworkz said Russia’s Noname057(16) threatened European operators this October — although groups route their operations through third-party countries.A wave of tech failures in recent weeks has shone a light on the vulnerability of other critical US digital infrastructure. A nationwide air traffic shutdown stranded hundreds of thousands of passengers a week ago, while a software glitch at Chase bank disrupted its banking systems on Monday, just days after Microsoft’s Outlook service went down for nearly 24 hours. None of these incidents have been linked to a cyber attack, but the chaos underlines the high stakes as rapid advances in AI could allow hackers to find and exploit vulnerabilities faster than companies can respond.
The FBI last week warned that hackers are using an AI tool named Artex to automate cyber attacks.

Corpus Christi port chief executive Kent Britton said attempted attacks have surged to a rate of “hundreds if not thousands” each day, from “known bad actor” states and organisations looking for high-profile targets. He declined to identify specific attackers.

Hackers are probing the port’s computer systems for weaknesses and sending fraudulent messages as senior executives to trick staff into allowing them access.“They’re poking at our systems and trying to find vulnerabilities,” Britton said. “With AI, it’ll only get more complicated.”

The threat is growing across the US. The US Coast Guard reported a 17 per cent increase in cyber maritime incidents last year and investigated cyber attacks on two US-bound oil tankers in August with the FBI.

The ships were carrying crude oil and liquefied petroleum gas from the Mediterranean to Galveston, Texas, when they were penetrated by hackers near the Strait of Gibraltar. Investigators have not publicly identified suspects.

The agencies said the joint offshore security boardings on August 21 and 24 were to “ensure integrity of the vessel’s operational and information technology systems following indications that the networks of both vessels were compromised”.
Coast guard officers board a tanker that was compromised by a cyberattack as it was delivering into Galveston, Texas in August

Should hackers breach ports, they could paralyse trade, disrupt energy exports and put lives at risk at sea. In August, North Carolina Ports said its IT systems had experienced a cyber attack by an “outside actor”. Although it was contained a day later, gate openings were delayed and the port had to switch to manual processing.

The Port of Los Angeles said it thwarted 120mn attempted attacks this August, nearly double the monthly average in 2023. This includes automated attempts to breach networks, gather passwords and install malware.
Maersk reported an intrusion this month in which hackers stole data, but said its operations weren’t impacted. The shipping giant said the incident was not a ransomware attack.

Ports are taking action to defend their waterways. The Port of Virginia, a major hub for consumer goods, agriculture and coal, said the threat of attacks is now “more acute because of the rise of AI”. It is heavily investing in its cyber security team, with employees undergoing monthly training and drills with the US Coast Guard. Spokesperson Joe Harris said the port had not yet suffered a successful breach, but warned of potentially disastrous consequences of an attack.
“We’re an economic pinch point,” he said. “Getting taken offline is not an option.”

The Port of Corpus Christi, which four years ago had no dedicated cyber security staff, is about to hire its fourth person. It also has a police department of roughly 50 officers and a coastguard unit. But it also has “very analogue” contingency plans should an attack breach its defences, Britton said.

Tugboats can escort ships through stretches of the channel, while the harbour master’s office can use two-way radios, binoculars, paper records and even hand signals to direct the flow of shipping traffic in an emergency.

The Port Authority of New York and New Jersey is also investing heavily in cyber defence. A spokesperson said it has “multiple independent layers of protection” and “recovery plans with terminal operators and partners, so that critical operations can continue and cargo can keep moving”.

Other ports are reluctant to discuss the threat they face — and their defences. The Port of Oakland said it would not publicly discuss its “cyber security defences or protective measures”, citing national security concerns.
Corpus Christi declined to provide further details on recent events but said it is seeking additional assistance from Washington.
“If you’re playing defence, you have to get it right every time,” Britton said. “If you’re planning offence, you only have get it right once.”

https://www.ft.com/content/08914b05-bbfa.lead_paragraph: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive in a stunning reversal of its position on the disgraced co-founder, sending the AI giant’s shares soaring more than 30 per cent in pre-market trading.
paragraphs: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive in a stunning reversal of its position on the disgraced co-founder, sending the AI giant’s shares soaring more than 30 per cent in pre-market trading.

In a statement on Monday, Nvidia said its board had voted unanimously to reinstate Huang “following a series of discussions and meetings . . . after which the board was satisfied with respect to Huang’s candor and ability to lead Nvidia”.

The Nvidia board said it received input from “senior levels” of the US government. “Based on that input, the board is confident that Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk,” the company added.

“The board believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers,” said Harvey Jones, chair of the board.
The company added that an investigation into Huang’s conduct was ongoing.

Until Monday, Nvidia’s stock had lost more than $2.5tn in value since its all-time high in October, before a series of revelations emerged about Huang’s affairs with at least one subordinate and with a client whom US intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy.
On Monday, Huang said he was “honoured to return to Nvidia”, which he co-founded 33 years ago. “I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” he said.

Despite the allegations against Huang and a series of state and federal investigations into Nvidia, US President Donald Trump has continued to stand by the AI company’s co-founder, saying he would like to see his friend and donor return as chief executive.
Trump said on Monday that Nvidia’s board made the “correct and proper decision” to return Huang to the role of CEO.

“The Country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,” Trump wrote in a social media post following the board’s announcement.

He added that the US government “has no reason” to believe that Huang’s return poses any risk to national security, adding that it “does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct”.

Trump said he that he has “gotten to know Jensen” and described him as a “Great Patriot and National Treasure”, adding that Nvidia should continue its investigation of its compliance with US export controls.

On Sunday, US Treasury secretary Scott Bessent seemingly reversed his position on Huang’s reappointment, refusing to rule out such a move after previously calling on the company’s board to implement a “dramatic shake-up” and look “outside” for new leadership.

The abrupt turnaround comes less than a week after Jones had told investors on Nvidia’s quarterly earnings call that the board had “unanimously accepted [Huang’s] resignation and does not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.

Several Silicon Valley investors and founders, including SpaceX and Tesla chief Elon Musk, investor Gavin Baker and former Uber chief Travis Kalanick, have pushed for Huang’s reinstatement. A petition to “bring Jensen back” has received more than 200,000 signatures, including from some Nvidia staff.
Nvidia shares opened 34 per cent higher on Monday morning, which, if sustained, would be the stock’s biggest one-day jump since March 2000.
Such a move would add about $1tn in market capitalisation, a record increase for any company, and follows a 14 per cent drop on Friday that wiped $492bn from the company’s valuation.

Huang thanked Nvidia’s board and Colette Kress, its finance chief who became interim CEO, as well as “employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support”.
“Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work,” he said.

https://www.ft.com/content/1e5a9d70-221d.summary: Comments from pharma CEO follow ambitious claims from Anthropic chief and DeepMind founder
https://www.ft.com/content/1e5a9d70-221d.author: Hannah Kuchler and Tim Bradshaw
https://www.ft.com/content/1e5a9d70-221d.lead_paragraph: Novartis chief executive and Anthropic board member Vas Narasimhan has rejected the idea that AI is going to cure cancer within five to 10 years, arguing it will take a decade to shave just four years off the process of drug development.
paragraphs: Novartis chief executive and Anthropic board member Vas Narasimhan has rejected the idea that AI is going to cure cancer within five to 10 years, arguing it will take a decade to shave just four years off the process of drug development.
Narasimhan said the tech industry approached the problem with an “engineering mindset”, but that clinicians and pharmaceutical companies could see how little we know about the human body.

“The real underlying issue we face is that we only understand about, we would argue, 5 per cent of what goes on in the human body,” he said. “In coding and in language we understand a much higher proportion and so the AI model’s ability to learn and predict is much higher.”

Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei has said AI will cure cancer and Alzheimer’s within a decade, while Sir Demis Hassabis, the Nobel Prize-winning founder of DeepMind and its drug discovery spin-off Isomorphic, said last year that he thought AI might be able to solve all diseases in as little as a decade.

The Swiss pharma group is using AI throughout its development process. It has found that AI has been most successful in accelerating early drug discovery, before a drug is tested in humans, where it could shave up to two years off a phase of development that usually took four, on average.

Narasimhan predicted that the use of AI could cut the whole process of drug development from an average of 12 years to an average of eight years within a decade. He said he hoped it could also improve the probability of a potential medicine being successful from 8 per cent of those that go into the first studies in humans to 12 per cent.

But he said the true impact of AI was probably “somewhere in the middle” of the ambitious predictions made by the AI companies and the view of the pharmaceutical industry, which has been more sceptical.
Several AI companies are trying to accelerate the laborious process of drug discovery and development.

Anthropic is investing in its own drug discovery programme, including buying small biotechs and building its own laboratories. Isomorphic, which announced last week that it had raised $5bn in its latest fundraising round, is collaborating with pharma companies on research programmes, including Novartis.
Speaking on Thursday when Anthropic made its stock market debut, Amodei said progress in curing many diseases has been “too slow”.

“Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades,” he said. “I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.”

Narasimhan said the debate with the AI industry relates to how long it will take to fill the vast gap in our knowledge of how the body works. AI could “unlock” a massive acceleration in the development process if regulators can be convinced we can predict how a drug will behave in a human with great certainty and so reduce requirements for trials.
But Narasimhan said he believed long clinical trials would still be required.
“I don’t think we’ll get away from the fact that in this period, you still need to put these medicines into animals and then humans to test the biological functions of these compounds,” he said.

https://www.ft.com/content/53d4b629-7ae4.title: EU plans €50bn tech fund to close gap with US and China
https://www.ft.com/content/53d4b629-7ae4.summary: Brussels plans to take stakes in AI and quantum computing companies to try to bolster Europe’s technological independence
https://www.ft.com/content/53d4b629-7ae4.author: Barbara Moens
https://www.ft.com/content/53d4b629-7ae4.lead_paragraph: The EU is drawing up plans to mobilise up to €50bn for a new fund that would make long-term, high-risk investments in European artificial intelligence and quantum computing companies, as Brussels seeks to reduce its dependence on US and Chinese technology.
paragraphs: The EU is drawing up plans to mobilise up to €50bn for a new fund that would make long-term, high-risk investments in European artificial intelligence and quantum computing companies, as Brussels seeks to reduce its dependence on US and Chinese technology.
The proposed Sovereign Tech Equity Fund (Stef) would make larger, riskier and longer-term investments than existing EU financing schemes, according to two officials involved in the discussions.
“These are long-term, stable investments in risky stuff,” one of the officials said. “It’s the opposite of what the EU usually does, which is exactly why we need it.”

The main focus of the investments will be in AI and quantum, which applies the principles of quantum mechanics to carry out calculations that are extremely difficult for conventional computers. The Commission will present a quantum strategy on Wednesday as it hopes to strengthen the bloc’s position in the emerging industry.
The new fund plans are part of a broader push to strengthen Europe’s technological independence amid growing uncertainty over US policy and an increasingly volatile geopolitical landscape.

Brussels also hopes to spur investment in emerging technologies where European companies have struggled to compete with their American and Chinese rivals. Stef investing in a company would encourage other investors to follow, the officials said.

Europe’s inability to fund and scale innovative tech companies is often cited as a key reason for the EU lagging behind the US and China, including in Mario Draghi’s recommendations on how to improve the bloc’s competitiveness.

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen promised an “ambitious proposal” to finance initiatives aimed at bolstering the bloc’s “tech sovereignty” after a discussion among leaders on AI earlier this month.

The goal is set to present operational details of the new fund in February, the officials said, when EU leaders will discuss the bloc’s competitiveness at a retreat in the Belgian town of Alden Biesen.

The precise financing of the fund is still being discussed. The Commission aims to use EU funds as seed money that would attract additional investment from the private sector, with the aim to mobilise as much as €6 for every euro committed, one of the officials said.
EU tech chief Henna Virkkunen already discussed the fund idea with the European Investment Bank last week. The bank could provide financial expertise without carrying the investment risk itself.
Virkkunen said at a conference last week the fund should aim to attract €50bn, which is a 10th of what the Commission estimates it will cost to achieve full tech sovereignty.
As with an existing Scaleup Europe Fund, Stef would be managed by an independent fund manager to ensure investment decisions were not subject to any political considerations.
Scaleup, which is available for the wider European tech sector, is managed by the Swedish private equity firm EQT and has a much lower fundraising target of €5bn.

Tech figures were quick to cheer Huang’s return, and dismiss fears about his conduct. “I hate to break it to you, but there are double standards for high performers,” venture capitalist and tech podcaster Jason Calacanis told Fox News.

A person close to commerce secretary Howard Lutnick, who brokered Huang’s introduction to Trump in 2025 and has remained close to the Nvidia executive, said he too had played no part.

On Monday, the commerce department blacklisted Megaspeed, the company that formerly employed Huang’s paramour Alice Huang, citing “significant risk of [the company] being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorized . . . end users”.
Huang’s few remaining allies in Washington also fear his resurrection may prove shortlived.

Congressional Republicans who once would have fallen into line behind the president’s decision made it clear that they would continue to investigate Nvidia and its chief executive. Several vowed to back tighter chip export controls in the must-pass defence budget bill, known as the NDAA.

If that fails, Democrats, who will be in the majority in both houses of Congress in January, might get enough Republicans onside for measures targeting Nvidia to override a veto from the president, a person working on legislation with Republicans said.

https://www.ft.com/content/049151e8-f97f.lead_paragraph: Four large adult content websites are seeking to reach a deal with the European Commission on preventing children from accessing porn, as the sites try to minimise upcoming fines under the bloc’s push to protect minors online.
paragraphs: Four large adult content websites are seeking to reach a deal with the European Commission on preventing children from accessing porn, as the sites try to minimise upcoming fines under the bloc’s push to protect minors online.

The Commission is investigating Pornhub, Stripchat, XNXX and XVideos for alleged breaches of the Digital Services Act by failing to adequately protect children from accessing adult content, as minors could access the porn platforms by simply claiming via one click that they are over 18. The DSA — which fully took effect in 2024 and forms part of the bloc’s broader digital rulebook — sets out how tech companies should police the internet.
The probe forms part of a broader European push to protect minors online that also includes a proposal to ban the use of social media, certain gaming platforms and AI chatbots by children under 13.

Since the start of the porn investigation in May last year, the four platforms have submitted co-ordinated commitments to address the concerns, but the Commission found those to be insufficient, two EU officials said.
The Commission is now discussing further remedies with the companies, although they are set to face fines for failing to take adequate measures in the past, the officials said.
Companies that fail to follow the EU digital rules face fines of up to 6 per cent of their global revenue, although the fines are rarely that high. The potential fines were first reported by MLex.

Brussels is simultaneously developing an EU-wide age-verification app that will allow all digital platforms, including porn websites, to confirm the age of a user without revealing additional personal information.

But it will take time to implement that technology, so the Commission is now discussing with the porn sites measures they can take to verify users’ ages in the transition phase. Any such measures would seek to avoid ongoing fines.
“We are looking into what we can accept,” one of the officials said.

The platforms have also raised concerns with the Commission that overly strict checks would lead adults to turn to lesser-known, smaller porn platforms which would be easier to access as they may have less strict age-verification systems.
To avoid this, EU member states have — in parallel with the EU probe — launched a co-ordinated crackdown on smaller platforms under national jurisdictions.
The companies did not immediately reply to a request for comment. The Commission declined to comment.
